books.section: Topic 4.6 Market Revolution: Society and Culture, C. Workers and New Methods of Production
The North and the Textile Industry

stimulus.text: Charles Dickens visited Lowell, Massachusetts, in 1842 and wrote about the mills in American Notes. He wrote that the mill girls were “well dressed,” healthy in appearance, and had “the manners and deportment of young women: not of degraded brutes of burden.” He added that “in July, 1841, no fewer than nine hundred and seventy-eight of these girls were depositors in the Lowell Savings Bank: the amount of whose joint savings was estimated at one hundred thousand dollars.” He closed by noting that “there is no manufacturing population in Lowell, so to speak: for these girls (often the daughters of small farmers) come from other States, remain a few years in the mills, and then go home for good.”
stimulus.source_note: Charles Dickens, American Notes (1842), Chapter 4. Passage paraphrased with short verbatim quotations; wording of quotations verified against the Project Gutenberg text.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Dickens's remark that the girls “remain a few years in the mills, and then go home for good” best explains why

options.text: the mills closed every winter for lack of water power
options.misconception: Dickens says the girls go home after a few years, not that the mills closed each winter.

options.text: mill owners refused to hire women who had worked in the mills before
options.misconception: The mills depended on a fresh supply of farm daughters; nothing says former workers were refused.

options.text: Lowell had no permanent class of factory workers in its early years
the girls were sent home when they married mill managers
options.misconception: Dickens says the girls went home after a few years, usually to marry and farm, not because they married managers.

rationales.A: Dickens describes a workforce that turns over, not a mill that shuts. The mills ran year-round on river power.
rationales.B: The mills needed new farm daughters every year as older ones left. Nothing in the passage says former workers were barred.
rationales.C: Dickens says the girls came from other states, stayed a few years, and then went home for good. A workforce that keeps turning over is not a permanent factory population.
rationales.D: The girls left to marry and return to farm life, not to marry managers. Dickens calls them daughters of small farmers going home.
rationales.general:
1. Read the sentence slowly. The girls come, stay a few years, and go home for good.
2. Ask what that means for the town. Each year brings new workers and loses old ones.
3. Name the result. Lowell had a passing workforce, not a settled factory class.
Background: Only in the 1840s, when Irish immigrants arrived, did Lowell gain a permanent mill workforce willing to stay for low wages.
Remember: when a writer says who comes and goes, ask what kind of community that movement makes.
